one_liner: D JSON library: parses to compact binary ASDF, binds typed structs; 1.16-1.46x faster than RapidJSON on kostya's JSON test.
what_it_does: A JSON parser and serializer for D (not C++) from the Mir project. It was first built at Tamedia to extract and transform real-time click streams. `parseJson` turns a string, or a range of byte chunks, into an `Asdf` value: a read-only binary tree you can query by key path (`data["a", "b"]`), iterate (`byElement`, `byKeyValue`) and print back to JSON, while `parseJsonByLine` streams JSON Lines. `deserialize!T` and `serializeToJson` map JSON to D structs and classes through compile-time reflection, with `@serde*` attributes for renaming, ignoring, proxies and transforms. It is a different language with a different API, so it does not replace RapidJSON in a C++ codebase.
how_it_is_fast: Parsing is a single goto-driven state machine. It turns JSON into ASDF, a length-prefixed binary format (a 1-byte type tag, uint32 lengths for strings, arrays and objects, and uint8 lengths for keys and numbers) written into one buffer allocated at 6x the input size. So there is no per-node allocation, and any subtree can be skipped by jumping over its length. With LDC and SSE4.2 enabled, strings and numbers are scanned 16 bytes at a time with PCMPISTRI; otherwise a 4x-unrolled lookup-table loop runs. Numbers stay as raw text until a field is bound, then go through Mir's precise decimal-to-float (`mir.bignum` decimalToFloatImpl), and struct binding is a compile-time-generated string switch over member keys, so undeclared keys are skipped without being decoded.
when_to_use: You are writing D with LDC and need JSON bound straight into typed structs or classes, not into a generic DOM.
Large files or high-volume JSON Lines (`parseJsonByLine`) where you read a few fields per record: undeclared keys and subtrees are skipped via their length prefixes.

Reduce-while-parsing jobs: the kostya benchmark streams each coordinate into a `put()` sink (`@serdeLikeList` + `@serdeProxy`), so the array is never built. It used 61 MiB of extra memory vs RapidJSON's 123-129 MiB.
You need correctly rounded doubles. kostya's notes list default RapidJSON and non-Mir D parsers as inexact on numbers, and asdf goes through Mir's precise decimal-to-float path.
Filtering or reshaping JSON records (key-path lookup, `remove()` to set a deleted bit, re-emit) without fully decoding each one.
when_not_to_use: C or C++ projects: there is no C API, so use yyjson or simdjson instead.
Maximum throughput: on the same kostya test, simdjson On-Demand (0.060 s), DAW JSON Link (0.070-0.089 s) and Rust serde (0.103-0.110 s) are all faster than asdf's 0.133 s.
Inputs with object keys longer than 255 bytes, numbers longer than 255 characters, or strings, arrays or objects over 2^32-1 bytes: the parser rejects them with an error.

Untrusted input that needs strict validation: raw bytes >= 0x80 are not UTF-8-validated, and number tokens are only checked against the character set `+-.0-9eE` while parsing, with the full grammar checked only when a field is converted.

Formats beyond JSON (Ion, MsgPack, YAML, CBOR) or a mutable DOM (`AsdfNode` can hold arrays only as leaf values): the Mir author's mir-ion covers those, though its Ion DOM was slower on kostya (0.220 s). Also weigh maturity: this is mostly a one-maintainer project with legacy Travis/AppVeyor CI configs.

integration.form: module (dub package `asdf`; a meson.build is also provided)
integration.dependencies: mir-algorithm (>=3.10.43), which pulls in mir-core; the D runtime/GC and Phobos (std.experimental.allocator)
integration.min_toolchain: Not documented. It needs a D compiler (DMD or LDC), and the SSE4.2 fast path needs LDC. The legacy CI matrix tested DMD 2.095.1 and LDC 1.25.1 plus the latest releases. The benchmark used LDC 1.41.0 with asdf ~>0.7.17 (0.7.x).
integration.platforms: x86-64, x86 and aarch64 (Linux and macOS in legacy Travis CI; Windows x64 in AppVeyor). SIMD is used only via SSE4.2 on x86 with LDC; every other target uses a scalar path.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. Each `parseJson` call owns its parser and output buffer, but `parseJsonByLine` reuses one internal buffer across lines.

gotchas: Struct fields are required by default. A missing key raises "non-optional member ... is missing" unless the field has `@serdeOptional`, while unknown keys are silently ignored.
`parseJson` allocates an output buffer of 6x the input length up front, from the GC by default. Pass a std.experimental.allocator allocator to control this.

`parseJsonByLine` reuses one buffer for every line, and by default silently skips invalid lines (`throwOnInvalidLines = No`). Values from `Asdf`, and strings from `@serdeScoped` or `const(char)[]` proxies, point into that buffer and become invalid once it moves on or is freed.

Floats: JSON `null` deserializes to NaN, the strings "nan" and "inf" are accepted, and `serializeToJson` writes NaN as the string "nan". A malformed float token throws a plain `Exception` ("Failed to deserialize number") instead of a SerdeException.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick asdf when your code is D. On kostya's test it ties gason (0.127-0.133 s) and yyjson (0.131-0.132 s), binds straight into typed structs with precise float parsing, and uses the least extra memory of the three (61 MiB vs 97 and 229 MiB). From C or C++, use yyjson or simdjson (whose On-Demand API is about 2.2x faster here); the repo's own old Haswell benchmark shows asdf's raw parse beating sajson 1.3-2.5x on 10 of 11 files but losing on nested.json.
verified_claims_summary: kostya/benchmarks' Json test parses a pretty-printed file of 524,288 coordinate records and averages x/y/z, on an Intel Xeon E-2324G in Docker, reporting medians ± MAD. asdf 0.7.x (LDC 1.41.0, dub release-nobounds, -mcpu=native, binding into typed structs) took 0.133 s, against a full RapidJSON Document at 0.154 s (g++ 16.1) and 0.194 s (clang++ 22.1/libc++, -O3 -march=native -flto). Against RapidJSON's full-precision mode (0.212/0.262 s) the margin grows to about 1.6-2.0x.
status_note: Low activity but still maintained by the Mir author: v0.8.0 was tagged 2025-11-06 after a compile fix, the package gets about 1.8k dub downloads a month, and it is BSL-1.0. However, CI still points at legacy Travis/AppVeyor, and the README's API-docs link (asdf.libmir.org) did not resolve on 2026-09-25.
